---
title: "Portfolio Constraints"
metadata:
  pagetitle: "Portfolio Constraints"
  description-meta: "How an investment policy statement becomes a feasible set in PortfolioAnalytics: box, group, weight-sum, return, position, leverage, factor and diversification constraints, their shadow prices, and which solver honors them."
---



How does an investment policy statement, written in prose by a committee,
become something a solver can read? @jagannathan2003 showed that the answer is
less mechanical than it looks: imposing a no-short-sale constraint on a
minimum-variance problem is mathematically the same as shrinking the covariance
matrix, so a constraint that binds is not a nuisance the optimizer works around
but information about which estimates it should not trust. @frost1988 had made
the empirical case fifteen years earlier, finding that bounding the weights
improved out-of-sample performance because it capped how much of an estimation
error any one position could express.

This chapter is about **strategic allocation** in the sense of
@sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory: the constraints are the policy,
the policy is set once from long-run beliefs, and @brinson1986 found that it
explains most of the variation in what a fund subsequently earns. We first set out what each
family of constraint does to the feasible set and what a binding constraint is
worth, then implement every constraint type `PortfolioAnalytics` offers on the
sixteen risky classes and record what each does to the two anchor portfolios of
@sec-09-mean-variance-implementation, then translate a complete mandate line by
line into a specification, solve it, audit it, and price each of its lines.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
R  <- as_xts_pm(sim_class_returns_monthly, date, class, return)   # 16 risky classes
rf <- sim_riskfree_monthly$return                                  # the bill
Re <- R - rf                                                       # excess returns
stopifnot(ncol(Re) == 16L, !anyNA(Re))
```
:::


## From Policy Statement to Feasible Set {#sec-12-constraints-theory}

Every constraint is a statement about which weight vectors are admissible. The
mean-variance problem of @markowitz1952, @eq-09-problem, is solved over the whole of
$\mathbb{R}^N$; a mandate replaces $\mathbb{R}^N$ by a feasible set
$\mathcal{C}$, and the constrained problem is

$$
\min_{\boldsymbol{w} \in \mathcal{C}} \; \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}
\qquad \text{or} \qquad
\max_{\boldsymbol{w} \in \mathcal{C}} \;
\frac{\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\mu}}{\sqrt{\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}}} .
$$ {#eq-12-problem}

@markowitz1956 solved exactly this problem for any set of linear constraints,
and the critical line algorithm of that paper is where the geometry of the
constrained frontier was first worked out; @perold1984 made it computable at
scale, and @kolm2014 survey the constraints practice has added since. The
families `PortfolioAnalytics` recognizes are these:

| Constraint | Feasible set | `add.constraint(type = )` | Convex |
|---|---|---|---|
| weight sum | $l_s \le \boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{w} \le u_s$ | `weight_sum`, `full_investment` ($=1$), `dollar_neutral` ($=0$) | yes |
| box | $l_i \le w_i \le u_i$ | `box`, `long_only` ($l_i = 0$) | yes |
| group | $l_g \le \sum_{i \in G_g} w_i \le u_g$ | `group` | yes |
| target return | $\boldsymbol{\mu}'\boldsymbol{w} = \bar{\mu}$ | `return` | yes |
| linear exposure | $\boldsymbol{l} \le \boldsymbol{B}'\boldsymbol{w} \le \boldsymbol{u}$ | `factor_exposure` | yes |
| leverage | $\lVert \boldsymbol{w} \rVert_1 \le L$ | `leverage_exposure` | yes |
| turnover, costs | $\lVert \boldsymbol{w} - \boldsymbol{w}_0 \rVert_1 \le \tau$ | `turnover`, `transaction_cost` | yes |
| diversification | $1 - \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{w} \ge d$ | `diversification` | yes |
| position limit | $\sum_i \mathbf{1}\{w_i \neq 0\} \le k$ | `position_limit` | **no** |

: The constraint families, the set each defines, and whether the set is convex. {#tbl-12-families}

The first seven rows are intersections of half-spaces, so any number of them
together leaves a convex set and @eq-12-problem remains a quadratic program
with a unique answer [@boyd2004]. The diversification floor is a ball
intersected with the simplex, also convex. Only the position limit breaks
convexity: the set of portfolios holding at most $k$ names is a union of faces
of the simplex, and @sec-13-solvers-theory shows what that costs in solver
choice. Turnover and transaction costs depend on a starting portfolio and have
their own chapter, @sec-23-rebalancing-theory.

### What a binding constraint is worth

Write the linear constraints as $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{w} \le \boldsymbol{b}$
and keep the budget separate. The Lagrangian of the minimum-variance problem is

$$
\mathcal{L}(\boldsymbol{w}, \lambda_0, \boldsymbol{\lambda})
= \tfrac{1}{2}\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}
- \lambda_0\left(\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\iota} - 1\right)
+ \boldsymbol{\lambda}'\left(\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{w} - \boldsymbol{b}\right),
$$ {#eq-12-lagrangian}

and the conditions of @kuhn1951 characterize the solution: at the optimum
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w} = \lambda_0\boldsymbol{\iota} - \boldsymbol{A}'\boldsymbol{\lambda}$,
every multiplier satisfies $\lambda_k \ge 0$, and
$\lambda_k\,(\boldsymbol{a}_k'\boldsymbol{w} - b_k) = 0$ for each row. The last
condition, complementary slackness, is the one to hold on to: a constraint
that is not binding has a multiplier of zero and could have been left out; a
constraint that binds has a positive multiplier, and that multiplier is its
**shadow price**,

$$
\lambda_k = -\,\frac{\partial\, \sigma^{2}_{*}/2}{\partial b_k},
$$ {#eq-12-shadow}

the rate at which the optimal variance would fall if the bound were relaxed by
one unit [@boyd2004, ch. 5]. Solvers do not always return the multipliers, but
@eq-12-shadow can be recovered by perturbing a bound and re-solving, which is
what @sec-12-constraints-application does for every line of a mandate.

### The Jagannathan--Ma covariance

For the long-only constraint $\boldsymbol{w} \ge \boldsymbol{0}$, with
multipliers $\boldsymbol{\delta} \ge \boldsymbol{0}$ so that the first-order
condition reads
$\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w} = \lambda_0\boldsymbol{\iota} + \boldsymbol{\delta}$,
@jagannathan2003 observed that the constrained solution is the *unconstrained*
minimum-variance portfolio of @eq-09-gmv computed on a modified matrix,

$$
\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}
= \boldsymbol{\Sigma} - \left(\boldsymbol{\delta}\boldsymbol{\iota}' + \boldsymbol{\iota}\boldsymbol{\delta}'\right),
\qquad
\boldsymbol{w}_{\text{long-only}}
= \frac{\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota}}
       {\boldsymbol{\iota}'\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota}} .
$$ {#eq-12-jm}

The proof is two lines: $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}\boldsymbol{w}
= \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w} - \boldsymbol{\delta}(\boldsymbol{\iota}'\boldsymbol{w})
- \boldsymbol{\iota}(\boldsymbol{\delta}'\boldsymbol{w}) = \lambda_0\boldsymbol{\iota}$,
using the budget and complementary slackness, and a vector proportional to
$\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}^{-1}\boldsymbol{\iota}$ is the unconstrained
answer. Element by element, $\tilde{\sigma}_{ij} = \sigma_{ij} - \delta_i - \delta_j$:
every covariance involving an asset the constraint excludes is reduced by that
asset's shadow price. The assets an unconstrained optimizer shorts are the ones
with high estimated covariance to the rest, and the constraint shrinks exactly
those covariances, which is why @jagannathan2003 could show that the long-only
minimum-variance portfolio performs about as well out of sample as one built on
a shrunk covariance of the kind @sec-07-covariance-matrix-theory estimates.
@demiguel2009a generalize the observation: a bound on the norm of the weight
vector is a family of shrinkage estimators indexed by the bound, with the
long-only constraint as one member. A binding constraint, on this reading, is
the mandate correcting the estimator.

### What constraints cost in information

The other side of the ledger is due to @grinold2000 and @clarke2002. The
fundamental law of active management, @grinold1989, says the attainable
information ratio is the product of forecasting skill and the number of
independent bets, and @clarke2002 add a third factor, the **transfer
coefficient**,

$$
\text{TC} = \operatorname{corr}\!\left(\sigma_i\, w^{c}_i,\; \sigma_i\, w^{u}_i\right),
$$ {#eq-12-tc}

the cross-sectional correlation between the risk-weighted positions the
constraints allow and the ones the forecasts called for. It is one when nothing
binds and falls with every constraint that does, and @eq-24-law in
@sec-24-benchmarks-and-active-risk-theory uses it to price a long-only
restriction on an active manager. @best1991 supply the mechanism: under bounds,
a small change in $\boldsymbol{\mu}$ no longer moves the weights continuously
but switches which constraints are active, so the data determine the *set* of
held assets and the bounds pin the weights within it. @michaud1989 and
@green1992, cited in @sec-09-mean-variance-implementation, describe the
unconstrained weights those bounds replace; @black1992 built an estimation
method around the observation that nobody would hold them. A tracking-error
limit is a constraint of the same family and is treated in
@sec-24-benchmarks-and-active-risk-theory following @jorion2003.

## Implementation {#sec-12-constraints-implementation}

### Two anchors and a bookkeeping function

Everything below is measured against the two anchor portfolios of
@sec-09-mean-variance-implementation, recomputed rather than retyped. The
tangency portfolio is requested with `maxSR = TRUE`, which
@sec-13-solvers-implementation verified against an independent solve.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
S  <- stats::cov(Re); mu <- colMeans(Re); N <- ncol(Re)
p_vol <- function(w) sqrt(as.numeric(t(w) %*% S %*% w) * 12)
p_ret <- function(w) sum(mu * w) * 12
p_sr  <- function(w) p_ret(w) / p_vol(w)

# Weights by name from any solved specification. The assertion is not
# decoration: a solver that fails returns NULL or NA without raising. A
# specification on part of the universe is solved on that part, and the
# series it leaves out come back with a weight of zero.
weights_of <- function(spec, method = "ROI", ...) {
  a <- names(spec$assets)
  stopifnot(all(a %in% colnames(Re)))
  w <- extractWeights(optimize.portfolio(Re[, a], spec, optimize_method = method, ...))
  stopifnot(!is.null(w), !anyNA(w), all(a %in% names(w)))
  out <- setNames(numeric(ncol(Re)), colnames(Re)); out[a] <- w[a]
  out
}
min_var  <- function(spec) weights_of(spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"))
tangency <- function(spec) weights_of(spec |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "StdDev"), maxSR = TRUE)

stats_of <- function(label, w) tibble::tibble(
  portfolio = label, vol = p_vol(w), ret = p_ret(w), sharpe = p_sr(w),
  held = sum(w > 1e-6), largest = max(w), in_what = names(which.max(w)))

base_spec <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only")

w_gmv <- min_var(base_spec)
w_tan <- tangency(base_spec)
anchors <- dplyr::bind_rows(stats_of("minimum variance", w_gmv),
                            stats_of("tangency", w_tan))
anchors
#> # A tibble: 2 × 7
#>   portfolio           vol    ret sharpe  held largest in_what      
#>   <chr>             <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <int>   <dbl> <chr>        
#> 1 minimum variance 0.0413 0.0329  0.795     6   0.821 US_government
#> 2 tangency         0.0512 0.0508  0.991     5   0.684 US_government
```
:::


The minimum-variance anchor places 82% in
US_government. That number is the reason this chapter exists, and
@sec-12-constraints-application returns to it.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked: the shadow prices of the long-only constraint, and @eq-12-jm checked

With the long-only anchor in hand, the multipliers can be read off the
first-order condition: $\boldsymbol{\delta} = \boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w} - \lambda_0\boldsymbol{\iota}$,
and $\lambda_0 = \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\Sigma}\boldsymbol{w}$ because
$\boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{\delta} = 0$ at the optimum.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
lambda0 <- as.numeric(t(w_gmv) %*% S %*% w_gmv)
delta   <- setNames(as.numeric(S %*% w_gmv) - lambda0, colnames(Re))
stopifnot(all(abs(delta[w_gmv > 1e-6]) < 1e-7), all(delta[w_gmv <= 1e-6] > 0))   # complementary slackness

S_tilde <- S - (outer(delta, rep(1, N)) + outer(rep(1, N), delta))       # @eq-12-jm
w_jm    <- as.numeric(solve(S_tilde, rep(1, N)))
w_jm    <- setNames(w_jm / sum(w_jm), colnames(Re))

c(max_abs_difference = max(abs(w_jm - w_gmv)),
  smallest_eigenvalue_ratio = min(eigen(S_tilde)$values) / min(eigen(S)$values))
#>        max_abs_difference smallest_eigenvalue_ratio 
#>       0.00000000000001816       1.00413189110421763
round(sort(delta * 12 * 1e4, decreasing = TRUE)[1:4], 2)      # largest, annualized variance x 1e4
#>     EU_credit     CH_credit     JP_credit CH_government 
#>          6.37          5.73          4.37          4.33
```
:::


The multipliers are zero on every held series and positive on every excluded
one, which is complementary slackness, and the unconstrained portfolio of
@eq-09-gmv on $\tilde{\boldsymbol{\Sigma}}$ reproduces the solver's answer to
2e-14. The largest shadow prices belong
to `EU_credit`, `CH_credit`, `JP_credit`.
Since $\delta_i$ is the covariance of series $i$ with the portfolio less the
portfolio's own variance, these are the series that covary most with what is
held, and theirs are the covariances @eq-12-jm shrinks most. The modified matrix stays positive
definite, its smallest eigenvalue within
0.41%
of that of $\boldsymbol{\Sigma}$.
:::

### Box constraints

A box constraint bounds each weight separately. `min` and `max` accept a
scalar or a vector named by asset, and a later box constraint replaces an
earlier one in the solved problem, which is how a cap is layered over
`long_only` here.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
bmax <- setNames(rep(0.25, N), colnames(Re))
bmax["GLOBAL_commodity"] <- 0.10                    # one class capped tighter
spec_box <- base_spec |> add.constraint(type = "box", min = 0, max = bmax)

w_gmv_box <- min_var(spec_box); w_tan_box <- tangency(spec_box)
dplyr::bind_rows(stats_of("minimum variance, 25% cap", w_gmv_box),
                 stats_of("tangency, 25% cap", w_tan_box))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 7
#>   portfolio                    vol    ret sharpe  held largest in_what  
#>   <chr>                      <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl> <int>   <dbl> <chr>    
#> 1 minimum variance, 25% cap 0.0526 0.0337  0.642     8    0.25 US_credit
#> 2 tangency, 25% cap         0.0698 0.0634  0.908     7    0.25 US_equity
```
:::


The cap binds hard on the minimum-variance side, where
82% in one series becomes
2 positions at exactly 25%, and volatility
rises from 4.13% to
5.26%. On the tangency side the Sharpe
ratio falls from 0.991 to
0.908.

### Group constraints

A group constraint bounds the sum of weights over a set of assets. The groups
are given as a list of index vectors and the limits as two vectors in the same
order, and nothing in the language enforces that order. `split()` returns its
groups alphabetically, so the limits are built by name and the order is
asserted, exactly as @sec-09-mean-variance-application did.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
group_of <- function(a) dplyr::case_when(
  grepl("_equity$", a)     ~ "equity",
  grepl("_government$", a) ~ "government",
  grepl("_credit$", a)     ~ "credit",
  TRUE                     ~ "commodity")
grp  <- split(seq_len(N), group_of(colnames(Re)))
gmin <- c(commodity = 0.00, credit = 0.05, equity = 0.20, government = 0.10)
gmax <- c(commodity = 0.15, credit = 0.40, equity = 0.60, government = 0.50)
stopifnot(identical(names(grp), names(gmin)), identical(names(grp), names(gmax)))

spec_group <- base_spec |>
  add.constraint(type = "group", groups = grp,
                 group_min = unname(gmin[names(grp)]),
                 group_max = unname(gmax[names(grp)]))

opt_group <- optimize.portfolio(Re, spec_group |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "StdDev"),
  optimize_method = "ROI", maxSR = TRUE)
w_tan_grp <- extractWeights(opt_group)[colnames(Re)]
w_gmv_grp <- min_var(spec_group)

extractGroups(opt_group)$group_weights
#>  commodity     credit     equity government 
#>    0.04136    0.16233    0.29630    0.50000
```
:::


`extractGroups()` returns the group sums by name; the chart is one call.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
chart.GroupWeights(opt_group, grouping = "groups", main = "")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![The package's own group chart for the tangency portfolio under class limits: each group's weight against its bounds. Base graphics, unstyled.](12-constraints_files/figure-html/fig-12-group-weights-1.png){#fig-12-group-weights fig-align='center' width=90%}
:::
:::



::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
g_tan <- extractGroups(opt_group)$group_weights[names(grp)]
g_gmv <- vapply(grp, function(i) sum(w_gmv_grp[i]), numeric(1))
tibble::tibble(group = names(grp), lower = gmin[names(grp)], upper = gmax[names(grp)],
               min_variance = g_gmv, tangency = g_tan) |>
  dplyr::mutate(binds_mv  = abs(min_variance - lower) < 1e-6 | abs(min_variance - upper) < 1e-6,
                binds_tan = abs(tangency - lower) < 1e-6 | abs(tangency - upper) < 1e-6)
#> # A tibble: 4 × 7
#>   group      lower upper min_variance tangency binds_mv binds_tan
#>   <chr>      <dbl> <dbl>        <dbl>    <dbl> <lgl>    <lgl>    
#> 1 commodity   0     0.15       0.0735   0.0414 FALSE    FALSE    
#> 2 credit      0.05  0.4        0.227    0.162  FALSE    FALSE    
#> 3 equity      0.2   0.6        0.2      0.296  TRUE     FALSE    
#> 4 government  0.1   0.5        0.5      0.5    TRUE     TRUE
```
:::


::: {.callout-note}
## One group constraint per specification

`add.constraint()` appends, but the solver reads constraints through
`get_constraints()`, which keeps only the *last* group constraint it meets, and
likewise the last box constraint. Regions on top of asset classes therefore
cannot be a second `group` line; the second grouping goes in as a linear
exposure constraint with an indicator matrix, shown below. The same rule is why
the box constraint above could replace `long_only` without complaint.
:::

### Weight-sum constraints

`full_investment` is `weight_sum` with both bounds at one; `dollar_neutral`
sets both to zero. A dollar-neutral minimum-variance portfolio is the zero
vector, so the long-short example needs a return term, here the quadratic
utility of @sec-03-return-risk-and-the-investor-theory with `risk_aversion`
read as $\gamma/2$.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
spec_dn <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "dollar_neutral") |>
  add.constraint(type = "box", min = -0.3, max = 0.3) |>
  add.objective(type = "return", name = "mean") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk",   name = "var", risk_aversion = 10)
w_dn <- weights_of(spec_dn)
round(c(sum = sum(w_dn), gross = sum(abs(w_dn)), longs = sum(w_dn > 1e-6), shorts = sum(w_dn < -1e-6)), 4)
#>    sum  gross  longs shorts 
#>  0.000  2.155  8.000  8.000
```
:::


::: {.callout-warning}
## `weight_sum` with no arguments leaves one percent uninvested

`weight_sum_constraint()` defaults to `min_sum = 0.99` and `max_sum = 1.01`,
chosen to give the random-portfolio sampler room. Under a variance objective
the solver uses that room:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
w_loose <- weights_of(portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "weight_sum") |>
  add.constraint(type = "long_only") |>
  add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"))
sum(w_loose)
#> [1] 0.99
```
:::


The weights sum to 0.99, which is a cash position
nobody asked for. Write `full_investment`, or write both bounds.
:::

### A target return

`return_constraint()` fixes $\boldsymbol{\mu}'\boldsymbol{w} = \bar{\mu}$, and
the word to notice is *fixes*. Under the ROI quadratic path the constraint is
an equality, so a target below the minimum-variance return drags the answer
onto the lower branch of the frontier.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
target_of <- function(ann) stats_of(sprintf("target %.1f%%", 100 * ann),
  min_var(base_spec |> add.constraint(type = "return", return_target = ann / 12)))
ret_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(stats_of("minimum variance, no target", w_gmv),
                            target_of(0.025), target_of(0.05))
ret_tbl[, c("portfolio", "vol", "ret", "sharpe")]
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   portfolio                      vol    ret sharpe
#>   <chr>                        <dbl>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 minimum variance, no target 0.0413 0.0329  0.795
#> 2 target 2.5%                 0.0434 0.025   0.576
#> 3 target 5.0%                 0.0505 0.05    0.991

stopifnot(0.025 < p_ret(w_gmv), p_ret(w_gmv) < 0.05)        # one target on each branch

w_tan_8 <- tangency(base_spec |> add.constraint(type = "return", return_target = 0.08 / 12))
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(w_tan_8, w_tan)))                # the target changed nothing
c(requested_under_maxSR = 0.08, achieved = p_ret(w_tan_8), tangency = p_ret(w_tan))
#> requested_under_maxSR              achieved              tangency 
#>               0.08000               0.05077               0.05077
```
:::


The 5% target is on the efficient branch: more return than the minimum-variance
portfolio for more risk. The 2.5% target delivers *less* return at
4.34% volatility against
4.13%, a portfolio the minimum-variance
anchor dominates. A mandate that says "at least" is a floor, and a floor
should be imposed only when it binds, which the audit at the end of this
section checks. The last line shows the second thing to know: `maxSR = TRUE`
ignores the constraint altogether, because `max_sr_opt()` searches over target
returns and overrides the one in the specification.

### Position limits

A cardinality constraint, at most $k$ non-zero weights, is the one row of
@tbl-12-families that is not convex, and @bienstock1996 shows that solving it
exactly is a mixed-integer quadratic program. `PortfolioAnalytics` accepts it
everywhere and honors it in three places.

::: {.callout-important}
## A position limit on the quadratic path is dropped without a message


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
spec_pos  <- base_spec |> add.constraint(type = "position_limit", max_pos = 5)
w_pos_roi <- min_var(spec_pos)
# the limit has to bind for this to be a test: the unconstrained answer holds more than five
stopifnot(sum(w_gmv > 1e-6) > 5, isTRUE(all.equal(w_pos_roi, w_gmv)))
c(limit = 5, held = sum(w_pos_roi > 1e-6), identical_to_unconstrained = isTRUE(all.equal(w_pos_roi, w_gmv)))
#>                      limit                       held 
#>                          5                          6 
#> identical_to_unconstrained 
#>                          1
```
:::


Under a variance objective the ROI path has no integer formulation, so the
constraint is read and then not used: 6 positions come
back under a limit of five. On the build this book pins, a position limit
(`max_pos`) on ROI's quadratic path is dropped without a message: no error, no
warning, and the unconstrained weights come back, exactly as on the CRAN
release. ROI honors the limit only on its two mixed-integer paths, maximum
return and minimum expected shortfall, which it hands to `Rglpk`. A patch that
refuses the quadratic call is proposed upstream, not in the pinned build
(@sec-93-package-notes). The honest check is `pos_limit_fail()`, which the
sampler uses internally and which takes any weight vector; the full table of
which solver honors which constraint is @sec-92-solver-matrix.
:::

The two paths on which ROI *does* honor the limit are linear, written as
mixed-integer programs. Minimum expected shortfall shows it on the same
specification:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
w_es     <- weights_of(base_spec |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "ES"))
w_pos_es <- weights_of(spec_pos  |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "ES"))
stopifnot(sum(w_es > 1e-6) > 5, !pos_limit_fail(w_pos_es, 5, NULL, NULL))   # binds, and is honored
c(held_without_limit = sum(w_es > 1e-6), held = sum(w_pos_es > 1e-6),
  fails_limit = pos_limit_fail(w_pos_es, 5, NULL, NULL))
#> held_without_limit               held        fails_limit 
#>                  6                  5                  0
```
:::


Under a variance objective the exact route does not exist in the package.
`DEoptim` and random portfolios repair every candidate through `rp_transform()`
until it satisfies the limit; `pso` and `GenSA` penalize the objective instead
and, on @sec-13-solvers-application's measurement, return the whole universe
anyway. A small seeded run of the one that works:


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1602)
# DEoptim prints its final member whatever `trace` says; capture.output() swallows it.
utils::capture.output(
  w_pos_de <- weights_of(spec_pos |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"),
                         method = "DEoptim", search_size = 2000, itermax = 50,
                         traceDE = 0, trace = FALSE)) |> invisible()

# The screening heuristic of Chang et al. (2000): keep the k largest
# unconstrained holdings and re-solve the quadratic program on them.
keep     <- names(sort(w_gmv, decreasing = TRUE))[1:5]
w_screen <- min_var(portfolio.spec(assets = keep) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |> add.constraint(type = "long_only"))
stopifnot(!pos_limit_fail(w_pos_de, 5, NULL, NULL), p_vol(w_pos_de) > p_vol(w_screen))
dplyr::bind_rows(stats_of("DEoptim, max 5", w_pos_de),
                 stats_of("screen then re-solve, 5", w_screen))[, c("portfolio", "vol", "held")]
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   portfolio                  vol  held
#>   <chr>                    <dbl> <int>
#> 1 DEoptim, max 5          0.0453     3
#> 2 screen then re-solve, 5 0.0414     5
```
:::


`DEoptim` honors the limit and lands at
4.53% volatility. The screening
heuristic of @chang2000, two lines and one quadratic program, reaches
4.14%. Neither is certified optimal;
the search is 9.5%
worse and far slower, which is @sec-13-solvers-application's point about
heuristics on this universe.

### Leverage exposure

`leverage_exposure_constraint()` bounds gross exposure $\lVert \boldsymbol{w} \rVert_1$,
the constraint that defines a 130/30 portfolio. It is convex: a bound on an
$\ell_1$ norm becomes linear once each weight is split into a long and a short
part, which is how the package writes it.

::: {.callout-important}
## Under ROI the leverage constraint returns a long-only portfolio


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
spec_ls  <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
  add.constraint(type = "box", min = -0.3, max = 1)
spec_lev <- spec_ls |> add.constraint(type = "leverage_exposure", leverage = 1.6)
w_lev_pa <- min_var(spec_lev)

# The same problem written directly, with no package in the loop.
w_var <- CVXR::Variable(N)
res_lev <- CVXR::psolve(CVXR::Problem(
  CVXR::Minimize(CVXR::quad_form(w_var, S)),
  list(CVXR::sum_entries(w_var) == 1, CVXR::p_norm(w_var, 1) <= 1.6,
       w_var >= -0.3, w_var <= 1)), solver = "OSQP")
w_lev_cvx <- setNames(as.numeric(CVXR::value(w_var)), colnames(Re))

w_lev_pacvx <- weights_of(spec_lev |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"), method = "CVXR")
# ROI returns the long-only answer; CVXR returns the answer to the box alone
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(w_lev_pa, w_gmv)), max(abs(w_lev_pacvx - min_var(spec_ls))) < 1e-3)

lev_tbl <- tibble::tibble(
  route  = c("PortfolioAnalytics, ROI", "PortfolioAnalytics, CVXR", "CVXR, written by hand"),
  gross  = c(sum(abs(w_lev_pa)), sum(abs(w_lev_pacvx)), sum(abs(w_lev_cvx))),
  shorts = c(sum(w_lev_pa < -1e-6), sum(w_lev_pacvx < -1e-6), sum(w_lev_cvx < -1e-6)),
  vol    = c(p_vol(w_lev_pa), p_vol(w_lev_pacvx), p_vol(w_lev_cvx)))
lev_tbl
#> # A tibble: 3 × 4
#>   route                    gross shorts    vol
#>   <chr>                    <dbl>  <int>  <dbl>
#> 1 PortfolioAnalytics, ROI   1         0 0.0413
#> 2 PortfolioAnalytics, CVXR  3.22      4 0.0398
#> 3 CVXR, written by hand     1.60      3 0.0403
```
:::


The package's ROI answer has gross exposure of exactly one and no short
position, and `all.equal()` confirms it is the long-only minimum-variance
portfolio (TRUE). The reason is in
`gmv_opt_leverage()`:
unlike `gmv_opt()`, it builds its `ROI::OP()` without a `bounds` argument, and
ROI's default bound on every variable is $x \ge 0$. The box minimum of $-0.3$ is
written into the constraint matrix and then overruled by a default nobody
wrote down. The direct solve, which is the same quadratic program with the
bounds stated, shorts 3 series, uses the full gross
budget and reaches a volatility
2.59 percent
lower. Under `optimize_method = "CVXR"` the constraint is not written at all
and the solver returns the box-only answer with gross exposure of
3.22. Until this is fixed upstream, a
leverage bound under a variance objective is a problem to write by hand.
:::

### Linear exposures, not only factor exposures

`factor_exposure_constraint()` bounds $\boldsymbol{B}'\boldsymbol{w}$ for any
matrix $\boldsymbol{B}$ with one row per asset. Betas are one use; an indicator
matrix is another, and it is how a second grouping enters beside the group
constraint above.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
region   <- sub("_.*$", "", colnames(Re))
B_region <- sapply(sort(unique(region)), function(r) as.numeric(region == r))
rownames(B_region) <- colnames(Re)
stopifnot(all(rowSums(B_region) == 1))

spec_region <- spec_group |>
  add.constraint(type = "factor_exposure", B = B_region,
                 lower = rep(0, ncol(B_region)), upper = rep(0.40, ncol(B_region)))
w_gmv_region <- min_var(spec_region)
round(as.numeric(t(B_region) %*% w_gmv_region) |> setNames(colnames(B_region)), 4)
#>     CH     EU GLOBAL     JP     UK     US 
#> 0.0530 0.0000 0.1157 0.2623 0.1690 0.4000
```
:::


With betas the same constraint bounds market exposure. The betas of
@sec-05-factor-models-implementation are recomputed in one line against an
equal-weighted composite of the five equity series.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
mkt_eq <- xts::xts(rowMeans(Re[, grepl("_equity$", colnames(Re))]), order.by = zoo::index(Re))
betas  <- vapply(colnames(Re), function(a)
  as.numeric(PerformanceAnalytics::CAPM.beta(Re[, a], mkt_eq, Rf = 0)), numeric(1))

spec_beta  <- base_spec |> add.constraint(type = "factor_exposure", B = betas, lower = 0.3, upper = 0.5)
w_gmv_beta <- min_var(spec_beta)
stopifnot(sum(betas * w_gmv) < 0.3, abs(sum(betas * w_gmv_beta) - 0.3) < 1e-6)   # the lower bound binds
c(beta_unconstrained = sum(betas * w_gmv), beta_constrained = sum(betas * w_gmv_beta),
  vol_unconstrained = p_vol(w_gmv), vol_constrained = p_vol(w_gmv_beta))
#> beta_unconstrained   beta_constrained  vol_unconstrained    vol_constrained 
#>            0.07924            0.30000            0.04133            0.05350
```
:::


The minimum-variance portfolio has a beta of
0.08 to the equity composite; asking for at
least 0.3 forces the solver to buy equity it did not want, and the lower bound
binds exactly. @sec-20-sustainability-implementation uses the same constraint
with a column of scores in place of betas.

### Diversification

`diversification_constraint()` asks for $1 - \boldsymbol{w}'\boldsymbol{w} \ge d$,
one minus the Herfindahl index of the weights. The floor is convex, but the
package routes it only to the search-based solvers, where it does two things
the documentation does not say.

::: {.callout-note}
## Under ROI the constraint is ignored; under the searches it is a band


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
spec_div  <- base_spec |> add.constraint(type = "diversification", div_target = 0.7)
w_div_roi <- min_var(spec_div)
stopifnot(diversification(w_gmv) < 0.7, isTRUE(all.equal(w_div_roi, w_gmv)))   # a target that binds, and is not read
c(diversification = diversification(w_div_roi), identical_to_unconstrained = isTRUE(all.equal(w_div_roi, w_gmv)))
#>            diversification identical_to_unconstrained 
#>                     0.3185                     1.0000
```
:::


The ROI path never reads `div_target`. The search-based path reads it inside
`constrained_objective()` as a penalty that fires only when the achieved value
is outside $[0.95\,d,\; 1.05\,d]$, so a target of 0.7 is satisfied by anything
between 0.665 and 0.735, and a portfolio *more* diversified
than the target is penalized too. It is a target, not a floor.
:::


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
set.seed(1602)
utils::capture.output(
  w_div_de <- weights_of(spec_div |> add.objective(type = "risk", name = "var"),
                         method = "DEoptim", search_size = 2000, itermax = 50,
                         traceDE = 0, trace = FALSE)) |> invisible()

# The floor as the convex constraint it is, w'w <= 1 - d, solved exactly.
res_div <- CVXR::psolve(CVXR::Problem(
  CVXR::Minimize(CVXR::quad_form(w_var, S)),
  list(CVXR::sum_entries(w_var) == 1, w_var >= 0, CVXR::sum_squares(w_var) <= 1 - 0.7)),
  solver = "CLARABEL")
w_div_cvx <- setNames(pmax(as.numeric(CVXR::value(w_var)), 0), colnames(Re))
# the search lands inside the band, below the target, and above the exact volatility
stopifnot(diversification(w_div_de) >= 0.95 * 0.7, diversification(w_div_de) < 0.7,
          p_vol(w_div_de) > p_vol(w_div_cvx))

tibble::tibble(route = c("DEoptim, target 0.7", "CVXR, floor 0.7"),
               diversification = c(diversification(w_div_de), diversification(w_div_cvx)),
               vol = c(p_vol(w_div_de), p_vol(w_div_cvx)))
#> # A tibble: 2 × 3
#>   route               diversification    vol
#>   <chr>                         <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 DEoptim, target 0.7           0.682 0.0536
#> 2 CVXR, floor 0.7               0.700 0.0456
```
:::


`DEoptim` returns a diversification of
0.682, inside the band and below the
target, at 5.36% volatility. The exact
solution of the floor sits at 0.700
with 4.56%. The search is not wrong
about the constraint; it is
18% worse on
the objective, which is @gilli2019's warning that a penalized heuristic solves
a different problem from the one written down. `HHI()` and `diversification()`
take any weight vector, and @sec-14-risk-based-allocation-theory uses them on
portfolios that were never optimized for either.

### Auditing a weight vector against its specification

Every failure above has the same shape: the constraint is in the object and
absent from the answer. The remedy reads the specification and checks the
weights against each line, extending the four-line `audit()` of
@sec-13-solvers-implementation to every constraint type.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
audit_spec <- function(w, spec, tol = 1e-6) {
  w <- w[names(spec$assets)]
  rows <- lapply(spec$constraints, function(cn) {
    if (!isTRUE(cn$enabled)) return(NULL)
    ok <- switch(cn$type,
      full_investment = , dollar_neutral = , active = , weight_sum = , leverage = , weight =
        sum(w) >= cn$min_sum - tol && sum(w) <= cn$max_sum + tol,
      box = , long_only = all(w >= cn$min - tol) && all(w <= cn$max + tol),
      group = { g <- vapply(cn$groups, function(i) sum(w[i]), numeric(1))
                all(g >= cn$cLO - tol & g <= cn$cUP + tol) },
      position_limit    = !pos_limit_fail(w, cn$max_pos, cn$max_pos_long, cn$max_pos_short),
      leverage_exposure = sum(abs(w)) <= cn$leverage + tol,
      factor_exposure   = { e <- as.numeric(t(cn$B) %*% w)
                            all(e >= cn$lower - tol & e <= cn$upper + tol) },
      return            = sum(mu * w) >= cn$return_target - tol,   # read as a floor
      diversification   = diversification(w) >= cn$div_target - tol,
      NA)
    tibble::tibble(constraint = cn$type, satisfied = ok)
  })
  dplyr::bind_rows(rows)
}

audit_spec(w_pos_roi, spec_pos)
#> # A tibble: 3 × 2
#>   constraint      satisfied
#>   <chr>           <lgl>    
#> 1 full_investment TRUE     
#> 2 long_only       TRUE     
#> 3 position_limit  FALSE
```
:::


The position limit the solver dropped is now a `FALSE` in a table rather than
a portfolio that looks finished. `chart.Weights()` draws the same information
for one optimization, with the box bounds as lines.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
chart.Weights(opt_group, main = "")
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![The package's `chart.Weights()` on the tangency portfolio under class limits. Base graphics, unstyled; the bound lines are the box constraint.](12-constraints_files/figure-html/fig-12-chart-weights-1.png){#fig-12-chart-weights fig-align='center' width=90%}
:::

## A Mandate, Line by Line {#sec-12-constraints-application}

### The policy statement

An endowment's investment committee writes, in prose: the portfolio is fully
invested and long only; equities between 40 and 60 percent; government bonds
at least 10 percent; credit at most 40 percent; commodities at most 15 percent;
no single class series above 35 percent; expected excess return at least 6
percent a year; at most eight positions. The first six lines are linear and
enter directly. The seventh is a floor, imposed only where it binds. The eighth
is the non-convex line, and the audit will say whether it matters.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
m_min <- c(commodity = 0.00, credit = 0.00, equity = 0.40, government = 0.10)
m_max <- c(commodity = 0.15, credit = 0.40, equity = 0.60, government = 1.00)
stopifnot(identical(names(grp), names(m_min)), identical(names(grp), names(m_max)))
floor_ann <- 0.06

mandate <- portfolio.spec(assets = colnames(Re)) |>
  add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>                 # fully invested
  add.constraint(type = "box", min = 0, max = 0.35) |>        # long only; no series above 35%
  add.constraint(type = "group", groups = grp,                # class limits, bound by name
                 group_min = unname(m_min[names(grp)]),
                 group_max = unname(m_max[names(grp)])) |>
  add.constraint(type = "position_limit", max_pos = 8)        # at most eight positions

# Does the return floor bind? Solve without it first.
w_m_gmv0 <- min_var(mandate)
stopifnot(p_ret(w_m_gmv0) < floor_ann)                        # it does
c(return_without_floor = p_ret(w_m_gmv0), floor = floor_ann)
#> return_without_floor                floor 
#>              0.05108              0.06000
```
:::


The minimum-variance portfolio under the first six lines earns
5.11%, below the
6% floor, so the floor binds on that
objective and is added as the equality it is. For the maximum-Sharpe objective
the constraint would be ignored anyway, so it is checked after the fact.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
mandate_r <- mandate |> add.constraint(type = "return", return_target = floor_ann / 12)
w_m_qp  <- min_var(mandate_r)                 # what the quadratic program returns
w_m_tan <- tangency(mandate)

audit <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  audit_spec(w_m_qp,  mandate_r) |> dplyr::mutate(objective = "minimum variance"),
  audit_spec(w_m_tan, mandate_r) |> dplyr::mutate(objective = "maximum Sharpe"))
failed <- dplyr::filter(audit, !satisfied)
# one line fails, on one objective: the limit the quadratic path dropped
stopifnot(identical(failed$constraint, "position_limit"),
          identical(failed$objective, "minimum variance"))
tidyr::pivot_wider(audit, names_from = objective, values_from = satisfied)
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   constraint      `minimum variance` `maximum Sharpe`
#>   <chr>           <lgl>              <lgl>           
#> 1 full_investment TRUE               TRUE            
#> 2 box             TRUE               TRUE            
#> 3 group           TRUE               TRUE            
#> 4 position_limit  FALSE              TRUE            
#> 5 return          TRUE               TRUE
```
:::


The tangency portfolio passes every line, including the two the solver never
read: it earns 6.58% against the
6% floor and holds
5 positions against a limit of eight. The
minimum-variance portfolio fails one line. It holds 10
positions, because the quadratic path dropped the limit as the callout above
said it would, and the audit is how one knows rather than hopes. The limit is
then imposed by the screen of @chang2000: keep the eight largest holdings and
re-solve the other seven lines on them.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
# The seven lines the solver reads, on any part of the universe.
build <- function(m_min, m_max, cap, floor, assets = colnames(Re)) {
  g <- split(seq_along(assets), group_of(assets))             # that part's own groups, by name
  stopifnot(all(names(m_min)[m_min > 0] %in% names(g)))       # no class with a floor is emptied
  portfolio.spec(assets = assets) |>
    add.constraint(type = "full_investment") |>
    add.constraint(type = "box", min = 0, max = cap) |>
    add.constraint(type = "group", groups = g,
                   group_min = unname(m_min[names(g)]), group_max = unname(m_max[names(g)])) |>
    add.constraint(type = "return", return_target = floor / 12)
}
keep8   <- names(sort(w_m_qp, decreasing = TRUE))[1:8]
w_m_gmv <- min_var(build(m_min, m_max, 0.35, floor_ann, assets = keep8))
stopifnot(all(audit_spec(w_m_gmv, mandate_r)$satisfied))      # every line, the eighth included
c(held = sum(w_m_gmv > 1e-6), vol_qp = p_vol(w_m_qp), vol_mandate = p_vol(w_m_gmv))
#>        held      vol_qp vol_mandate 
#>     8.00000     0.06584     0.06594
```
:::


The repaired portfolio passes every line, and the eighth line costs
0.010 percentage points
of volatility for the 2 positions
it removes. The screen is a heuristic, so that figure is an upper bound on the
price of the line.


::: {#tbl-12-mandate .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='The mandate against the unconstrained anchors of chapter 9. All figures annualized, in excess of the bill.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}


|                                | volatility| excess return| Sharpe| held| largest|in            |
|:-------------------------------|----------:|-------------:|------:|----:|-------:|:-------------|
|minimum variance, unconstrained |      4.13%|         3.29%|  0.795|    6|     82%|US_government |
|minimum variance, mandate       |      6.59%|         6.00%|  0.910|    8|     35%|US_government |
|tangency, unconstrained         |      5.12%|         5.08%|  0.991|    5|     68%|US_government |
|tangency, mandate               |      7.07%|         6.58%|  0.931|    5|     35%|US_government |

### Which lines bind, and what each is worth

Complementary slackness says a slack constraint has a shadow price of zero.
@eq-12-shadow is recovered by tightening each line by one percentage point and
re-solving, the finite-difference version of the multiplier; the cardinality
line is left out because the solver does not read it, so the baseline is the
quadratic program's answer to the other seven, and the repair above is the
price of the eighth.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
tighten <- list(
  `equity >= 40%`     = \(m1, m2, cap, fl) { m1["equity"] <- m1["equity"] + 0.01;         build(m1, m2, cap, fl) },
  `equity <= 60%`     = \(m1, m2, cap, fl) { m2["equity"] <- m2["equity"] - 0.01;         build(m1, m2, cap, fl) },
  `government >= 10%` = \(m1, m2, cap, fl) { m1["government"] <- m1["government"] + 0.01; build(m1, m2, cap, fl) },
  `credit <= 40%`     = \(m1, m2, cap, fl) { m2["credit"] <- m2["credit"] - 0.01;         build(m1, m2, cap, fl) },
  `commodity <= 15%`  = \(m1, m2, cap, fl) { m2["commodity"] <- m2["commodity"] - 0.01;   build(m1, m2, cap, fl) },
  `no series > 35%`   = \(m1, m2, cap, fl) build(m1, m2, cap - 0.01, fl),
  `return >= 6%`      = \(m1, m2, cap, fl) build(m1, m2, cap, fl + 0.01))

stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(min_var(build(m_min, m_max, 0.35, floor_ann)), w_m_qp)))   # same seven lines
shadow <- lapply(names(tighten), function(nm) {
  s <- tighten[[nm]](m_min, m_max, 0.35, floor_ann)
  tibble::tibble(line = nm,
                 d_vol_mv  = 100 * (p_vol(min_var(s)) - p_vol(w_m_qp)),
                 d_sr_tan  = p_sr(tangency(s)) - p_sr(w_m_tan))
}) |> dplyr::bind_rows()
```
:::



::: {#tbl-12-shadow .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Finite-difference shadow prices: the change in minimum-variance volatility (percentage points) and in the maximum Sharpe ratio when each line is tightened by one percentage point. A zero is a slack constraint.'}
::: {.cell-output-display}

|:-----------------|--------------------------:|:-----|------------------:|:-----|
|equity >= 40%     |                     +0.045|binds |            -0.0023|binds |
|equity <= 60%     |                     +0.000|slack |            +0.0000|slack |
|government >= 10% |                     +0.000|slack |            -0.0000|slack |
|credit <= 40%     |                     +0.000|slack |            +0.0000|slack |
|commodity <= 15%  |                     +0.000|slack |            +0.0000|slack |
|no series > 35%   |                     +0.020|binds |            -0.0018|binds |

Of the seven lines priced, 3 bind on the minimum-variance
objective (equity >= 40%; no series > 35%; return >= 6%) and 2 on the
tangency (equity >= 40%; no series > 35%). The rest cost nothing in
sample, which is not the same as costing nothing: a slack line is insurance
against a future estimate that would make it bind. The most expensive line for
the minimum-variance portfolio is return >= 6%, at
1.037 percentage
points of volatility per point of tightening; for the tangency it is
equity >= 40%, at
0.0023 of Sharpe
ratio per point.

### What the mandate costs, and what it buys


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
sig <- sqrt(diag(S))
tc  <- stats::cor(sig * w_m_tan, sig * w_tan)               # @eq-12-tc
stopifnot(p_sr(w_m_tan) < p_sr(w_tan), identical(names(which.max(w_m_tan)), names(which.max(w_tan))))
c(sharpe_unconstrained = p_sr(w_tan), sharpe_mandate = p_sr(w_m_tan),
  kept = p_sr(w_m_tan) / p_sr(w_tan), transfer_coefficient = tc)
#> sharpe_unconstrained       sharpe_mandate                 kept 
#>               0.9910               0.9311               0.9395 
#> transfer_coefficient 
#>               0.8366
```
:::


In sample the mandate costs 0.060
of Sharpe ratio, keeping 94%
of the unconstrained figure, with a transfer coefficient of
0.84 in the sense of @eq-12-tc. What it buys is a
portfolio: the unconstrained tangency held
68% in US_government, and the
mandate caps that at 35%. The in-sample
cost is the number @sec-08-estimation-error-theory taught us to distrust most:
it is measured against a tangency portfolio whose Sharpe ratio is itself
inflated by estimation error, so part of what the constraint "costs" is noise
it refused to buy, which is @jagannathan2003's point in Sharpe units.


::: {.cell layout-align="center"}

```{.r .cell-code}
rung_w <- function(label, w_mv, w_tn) dplyr::bind_rows(
  tibble::tibble(rung = label, objective = "minimum variance", asset = colnames(Re), weight = w_mv[colnames(Re)]),
  tibble::tibble(rung = label, objective = "maximum Sharpe",   asset = colnames(Re), weight = w_tn[colnames(Re)]))
rung <- function(label, spec_mv, spec_tan) rung_w(label, min_var(spec_mv), tangency(spec_tan))

cap_spec <- base_spec |> add.constraint(type = "box", min = 0, max = 0.35)
grp_spec <- cap_spec  |> add.constraint(type = "group", groups = grp,
                                        group_min = unname(m_min[names(grp)]),
                                        group_max = unname(m_max[names(grp)]))
ladder <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  rung("1 long only",        base_spec, base_spec),
```

### Why the constraints come first

Read the left panel of @fig-12-ladder from the first rung. Unconstrained
minimum variance on this universe is degenerate: it puts
82% into US_government, holds
6 series, and is the answer @green1992 predict whenever one
asset has a volatility far below the rest, which
@sec-09-mean-variance-implementation measured at
4.4
times between the most and least volatile. The 35% cap pins
US_government at the cap and spreads the remainder over
6 further series, still
55% in government
bonds. Only the class limits produce a portfolio a committee would
recognize, with 8 positions and equity at
40% of the total. On this
universe the group constraints are not a refinement of the optimization; they
are the precondition for a portfolio anyone would hold, and the estimation
error @sec-08-estimation-error-theory measured is why the constrained answer,
not the unconstrained one, is the honest estimate. That the same constraints
are where a sleeve structure comes from is the subject of
@sec-15-hierarchical-allocation-theory.

## Key Takeaways {.unnumbered}

- A constraint defines the feasible set, and every family in @tbl-12-families
  except the position limit keeps it convex. Choosing a constraint chooses the
  solver: a position limit needs a mixed-integer formulation or a heuristic,
  and @sec-13-solvers-theory measures what the heuristic is worth.
- A binding long-only constraint is equivalent to shrinking the covariance
  matrix by the constraint's own shadow prices, @eq-12-jm [@jagannathan2003],
  so a constraint that binds is the mandate correcting the estimator rather
  than a cost to be minimized.
- Shadow prices are recovered by tightening each line and re-solving. On the
  mandate here most lines are slack in sample: the equity floor and the 35%
  cap bind on both objectives and the return floor is the most expensive line
  for minimum variance. The cardinality limit is slack for the tangency
  portfolio and violated by the minimum-variance answer, where the quadratic
  path drops it and a screen has to impose it.
- `PortfolioAnalytics` accepts every constraint on every solver and honors only
  some. On the build this book pins, the ROI quadratic path drops a position
  limit and a diversification target silently, `maxSR = TRUE` ignores a return
  target, and a leverage bound returns a long-only portfolio because
  `gmv_opt_leverage()` omits ROI's variable bounds.
- Audit every returned weight vector against the specification it came from:
  `extractGroups()`, `HHI()`, `diversification()`, `pos_limit_fail()` and the
  sum of weights, or `audit_spec()` above, which reads the specification and
  checks each line.
